issues: 黑嶺已來 read as "from the Black Ridge onwards" (i.e. beyond it); 已來 means the region on this side of, up to, the Black Ridge
en_revised: Up to the Black Ridge (Heiling), all are customs of the Hu. Although they are grouped with the Rong peoples, they are divided into distinct tribes with demarcated borders, and for the most part, they are settled inhabitants. They build walled cities and devote themselves to agriculture and animal husbandry. By nature, they value wealth and property, while their customs hold benevolence and righteousness in low regard. There is no ritual in marriage, and no order of precedence between the noble and the base; the words of women are heeded, while men occupy a subordinate position. Upon death, they cremate the remains, and there is no fixed period for mourning. They scarify their faces and mutilate their ears, cut their hair and rend their garments, and slaughter herds of livestock to sacrifice to the spirits of the dead. On auspicious occasions they wear white garments, while for mourning they dress in black. These are the general customs and practices, briefly outlined here; their differing administrations and unique regulations will be described separately according to each region. The customs of India are discussed in the final record.
li_quote: Up to the Black Range, the customs of the Hu people are prevalent.

issues: 微有繒絹 rendered "There is a little silk": CBETA's 繒絹 is a corruption of 增損 (Ji 1985 adopts 增損 from the other witnesses; cf. Kuci's parallel 粗有改變); the phrase qualifies the script: "with slight modifications"
en_revised: The kingdom of Agni (阿耆尼國) is over six hundred *li* from east to west and over four hundred *li* from south to north. The kingdom’s capital city is six or seven *li* in circumference. It is backed by mountains on all four sides, and the roads are perilous and easy to defend. Streams flow around it, and water is diverted to irrigate the fields. The soil is suitable for growing non-glutinous millet, broomcorn millet, winter wheat, fragrant jujubes, grapes, pears, crabapples, and various other fruits. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs of the people are simple and honest. Their writing system is modeled on that of India, with slight modifications (reading 增損 for CBETA's 繒絹 "silk"). Their clothing is made of felt and coarse wool; they cut their hair short and do not wear headcloths. For currency, they use gold coins, silver coins, and small copper coins. The king is a native of the country; he is brave but lacks strategy, and he is fond of boasting of his own achievements. The country lacks a strict code of conduct, and the laws are not well-regulated. There are more than ten monasteries with over two thousand monks, who study the Sarvāstivāda (說一切有部) school of the Hīnayāna. Since their scriptural teachings and Vinaya discipline follow those of India, the students study them using the original texts. Their conduct and adherence to the Vinaya are pure, clean, and diligent. However, they consume the three kinds of "pure meat," remaining attached to the gradual teachings.
li_quote: Their alphabet is taken from that of India with slight modiﬁcations.

issues: 潔清耽翫，人以功競 rendered "devoted to cleanliness and purity, and the people compete in meritorious deeds": 耽翫 is being engrossed in study (cf. 即其文而翫之 for Agni), dropped; 功競 is vying in attainment
en_revised: Traveling southwest from here for over two hundred li, crossing a small mountain and two large rivers, I reached a plain to the west; after traveling over seven hundred li, I arrived at the country of Kuci (屈支國) (formerly called Qiuci 龜茲). The country of Kuci is over one thousand li from east to west and over six hundred li from south to north. The capital city is seventeen or eighteen li in circuit. The soil is suitable for millet and wheat, and there is round-grained rice; it produces grapes and pomegranates, and abounds in pears, crabapples, peaches, and apricots. The land produces gold, copper, iron, lead, and tin. The climate is temperate, and the customs are simple. Their writing system is modeled on that of India, with slight modifications. In string and wind music, they are especially superior to other countries. Their clothing is made of brocade and felt, and they cut their hair and wear turbans and caps. For currency, they use gold coins, silver coins, and small copper coins. The king is of Kuci stock; he is of little wisdom and is constrained by powerful ministers. It is their custom that when a child is born, they press its head with a wooden board, wishing it to be flat. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas (伽藍) with more than five thousand monks, who study the Hīnayāna teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school. Their scriptural teachings and monastic regulations are modeled on those of India, and those who study them read the original texts. They still adhere to the gradual teachings and consume the three kinds of pure meat. They are pure in conduct and engrossed in study, and they vie with one another in attainment.
li_quote: But they are pure in conduct and deeply engrossed in studies, and they compete with one another in their achievement of spiritual cultivation.

issues: 會場 rendered "assembly hall": it is the assembly ground in front of the two standing statues outside the west gate (建五年一大會處), not a hall
en_revised: Northwest of the assembly ground, one crosses a river to reach the Āścarya monastery (the Chinese name means "Marvelous"). The courtyards and buildings are spacious and bright, and the Buddha images are skillfully adorned. The monks are solemn and respectful, diligent and untiring; they are all elders of great virtue, profound learning, and high talent, and outstanding individuals from distant regions who have come here out of admiration for the truth. The king, ministers, scholars, commoners, and the wealthy and influential provide the four requisites of support, and their reverence only increases with time.  I have heard from the records of former times that a previous king of this country, who deeply revered the Triple Gem, wished to travel abroad to pay homage to holy sites, so he commanded his younger brother by the same mother to act as regent and oversee state affairs. Upon receiving this command, the brother secretly castrated himself to prevent any future suspicion. He sealed the organ in a golden casket and presented it to the king. The king asked, "What is the meaning of this?" He replied, "You may open it on the day you return." The king then entrusted it to an attendant to be kept safe with the royal retinue.  Upon the king’s return, there were indeed those who slandered him, saying, "While the king ordered him to oversee the state, he has been engaging in illicit relations within the inner palace." Hearing this, the king was enraged and intended to impose a severe punishment. The brother said, "I dare not evade the charge, but I ask that you open the golden casket." The king then opened it and looked inside, and it was his severed organ. The king asked, "What is this strange object? What are you trying to demonstrate?" He replied, "When Your Majesty went on a tour in the past and ordered me to handle affairs in your absence, I feared the disaster of slander, so I castrated myself to prove my innocence. Now that the accusation has indeed arisen, I ask that you examine this." The king was deeply astonished and moved, and his affection for him grew even greater; he was permitted to enter and leave the inner palace without any restrictions. Later, the king’s younger brother was traveling when he encountered a man driving five hundred bulls, intending to have them castrated. Seeing this, he reflected on their shared plight and his heart was filled with emotion: "That I am now physically deformed, is it not due to my past karma?" He immediately used his wealth and jewels to redeem this herd of cattle. Through the power of his compassion, his male form was gradually restored. Because his form was restored, he subsequently ceased entering the inner palace. The king, finding this strange, asked him about it, and he then explained the beginning and the end of the matter. The king considered this a marvelous event and subsequently built a monastery to commemorate this noble deed and transmit his fame to future generations.
li_quote: At the northwest of the meeting place I crossed a river and reached Āścarya (“Marvelous”) Monastery.

issues: 唐言守安國 rendered "Shou'an": CBETA's 守 is a corruption of 中 (Ji 1985 restores 中 from the other witnesses, with the Cien zhuan); Bukhārā is 中安國, Middle An, between 東安國 (Kharghānkath) and 西安國 (Betik)
en_revised: From this country, proceeding westward for more than four hundred li, one reaches the country of Buhe (捕喝國) (in the language of the Tang, this is called the country of Zhong'an, Middle An; reading 中 for CBETA's 守). The country of Buhe is sixteen or seventeen hundred li in circuit; it is long from east to west and narrow from south to north. Its soil, products, and customs are the same as those of the country of Samarkand (颯秣建國).
li_quote: Bukhārā (known as Middle Anguo in Chinese)

issues: 南北三百餘里 rendered "three hundred li": 餘 ("over") dropped
en_revised: Traveling south from the country of Bactria (縛喝國) for over one hundred li, one arrives at the country of Gachi (揭職國). The country of Gachi is over five hundred li from east to west and over three hundred li from north to south. The capital city is four or five li in circuit; the land is stony and barren, with a succession of hills and mounds. There are few flowers or fruits, but much pulse and wheat. The climate is cold and severe, and the customs of the people are fierce and violent. There are more than ten monasteries and over three hundred monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school. To the southeast, one enters the Great Snow Mountains (Mahāhimavat), where the valleys are deep and the mountains high, and the peaks and cliffs are treacherous. Wind and snow follow one another, and even in midsummer, it remains frozen; accumulated snow fills the valleys, and the paths are difficult to traverse. Mountain spirits and demons act with violent malice, and bands of robbers roam freely, making murder their occupation.
li_quote: over three hundred li from south to north

issues: 服用毛㲲，衣兼皮褐 rendered "garments of wool and clothing made of leather and felt": 㲲 (cotton) dropped
en_revised: From here, traveling east, one enters the Snow Mountains (Himālaya), crosses the Black Range (黑嶺), and arrives at the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國). The country of Kāpiśī is over four thousand li in circuit; it has the Snow Mountains at its back to the north and is bordered on three sides by the Black Range. The capital city of the country is over ten li in circuit. The land is suitable for grain and wheat, and produces many fruits and trees; it yields fine horses and saffron. Rare goods from various regions are mostly gathered in this country. The climate is cold and windy; the people’s nature is violent and rough, their speech is vulgar, and their marriage customs are chaotic. Their writing is largely the same as that of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國), though their customs, language, and manners of instruction are quite different. They wear garments of wool and cotton, and also clothing made of leather and felt. For currency, they use gold coins, silver coins, and small copper coins, the standards and designs of which differ from those of other countries. The king is of the Kṣatriya caste; he is wise and resourceful, brave and fierce by nature, and his might intimidates the neighboring regions, ruling over ten or more countries. He loves and nurtures his subjects and reveres the Triple Gem. Every year, he commissions a silver Buddha image eighteen feet high and holds an unrestricted great assembly (無遮大會) to provide for the poor and destitute and bestow alms upon widowers and widows. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas, with more than six thousand monks, who mostly study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. The stūpas and saṃghārāmas are lofty, spacious, vast, and pure. There are several dozen deva temples and over one thousand followers of heterodox paths; some go naked, some smear themselves with ash, and some wear garlands of skulls as crowns.
li_quote: They wear woolen and cotton clothes and also use fur and hemp in making garments.

issues: 河西蕃維 rendered "the vassal states west of the river": 河西 is the Hexi region, west of the Yellow River (the frontier of China; hence the princes' Chinese dress, 頗同中夏)
en_revised: Three or four li to the east of the great city, at the foot of the northern mountain, there is a large monastery with over three hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). According to the records of former times, King Kaniṣka of the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) once extended his prestige to neighboring countries and his influence to distant regions. He mobilized his army to expand his territory as far as the east of the Pamirs (葱嶺), and the vassal states of Hexi (河西, west of the Yellow River), fearing his might, sent hostages to him. Having received the hostage princes, King Kaniṣka treated them with special courtesy and provided them with different residences according to the seasons: in winter they stayed in the various states of India, in summer they returned to the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國), and in spring and autumn they resided in the country of Gandhāra. Because the hostage princes had residences for these three seasons, a monastery was built for each; this monastery is the one built for their summer residence. Therefore, on the walls of the various buildings, the hostage princes are depicted, their appearance and attire quite similar to those of the Middle Kingdom (China). After they were able to return to their own countries, they kept their former residences in their hearts, and although separated by mountains and rivers, they did not cease their offerings. Thus, the present community of monks, whenever the time comes for the entry into or the conclusion of the summer retreat, holds grand Dharma assemblies to pray for blessings and cultivate merit for the sake of the hostage princes, a practice that has continued without interruption to the present day. Beneath the right foot of the statue of the Great Spirit King, located to the south of the east gate of the monastery’s Buddha hall, there is treasure buried in the ground, hidden there by the hostage princes. The inscription regarding this says: "When the monastery falls into disrepair, take this to restore it." Recently, a frontier king, greedy and fierce, heard that this monastery contained much hidden treasure and drove out the monks. Just as he was about to begin the excavation, the figure of a parrot on the crown of the Divine King vigorously flapped its wings and cried out in alarm, causing the earth to shake; the king and his soldiers fell back in terror and collapsed, and only after a long time could they rise, whereupon they apologized for their offense and returned home. On the northern ridge of the monastery there are several stone chambers, which are the places where the hostage princes practiced meditation. Within them are hidden many miscellaneous treasures, and beside them is an inscription, guarded by a yakṣa. Whenever anyone wished to open them and take the treasures within, this yakṣa would manifest various forms through supernatural power—appearing as a lion, a python, a fierce beast, or a poisonous insect—showing great wrath in these strange forms, so that no one dared to attempt an excavation. On a great mountain ridge two or three li to the west of the stone chambers, there is a statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara; if someone prays with utmost sincerity to see him, the Bodhisattva emerges from the statue in a wondrous physical form to comfort the practitioner.
li_quote: the lord of a Chinese vassal state west of the Yellow River sent his son as hostage to the king

issues: 今有先獻者，願垂恩賜 rendered "There is someone who will offer something today; I hope for your grace to bestow it upon me": the minister asks for whatever is offered first (先獻) that day, which is why he waits at the gate for the first comer
en_revised: Thirty-some *li* southeast of the great city, one arrives at the Rāhula (曷邏怙羅) monastery. Beside it is a *stūpa* over one hundred feet high. On days of fasting, it sometimes emits a bright light. From the crevices in the stone of the inverted-bowl structure, black fragrant oil flows out, and in the quiet of the night, sounds of music are sometimes heard. According to ancient records, it was built in the past by Rāhula, a high minister of this country. After the work was completed, someone spoke to him in a dream, saying, "The *stūpa* you have built does not yet contain any relics. Tomorrow morning, someone will offer one; you should request it from the king." At dawn, he entered the court and made his request, saying, "Unaware of my own mediocrity, I dare to make a petition." The king asked, "What is it that you desire?" He replied, "I hope for your grace to bestow on me whatever is first offered to you today." The king said, "Very well." Rāhula stood waiting at the palace gate, watching for the arrival. Soon, a man appeared carrying a relic casket. The minister asked, "What do you intend to offer?" The man replied, "Buddha relics." The minister said, "I will guard them for you; you should first report this to the king." Fearing that the king would prize the relics and regret his previous favor, Rāhula hurried to the monastery and climbed the *stūpa*. Moved by his utmost sincerity, the stone inverted bowl opened of its own accord. He placed the relics inside and rushed out so quickly that his clothes were caught. The king sent men to pursue him, but the stone had already closed. Therefore, black fragrant oil flows from its crevices.
li_quote: “Will Your Majesty grant me what is ﬁrst offered to you today?”

issues: 叩王象而諫 rendered "knocked on the king's elephant": 叩 here is 叩馬而諫, seizing the mount to stop it and remonstrate
en_revised: Two hundred and more *li* northwest of the royal city, one arrives at the Great Snowy Mountain (Mahāhimavat). On the summit of the mountain is a pool; those who pray for rain or for clear weather have their wishes fulfilled according to their requests. According to ancient records, there was formerly an arhat in the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) who regularly received offerings from the nāga king of this pool. Every day at the midday meal, he would use his supernatural powers to sit upon his rope bed and travel through the void. His attendant, a novice (śrāmaṇera), secretly clung to the underside of the rope bed and hid himself. When the time for the meal arrived, the arhat departed; upon reaching the nāga palace, he discovered the novice. The nāga king then invited them both to stay for the meal. The nāga king served the arhat with heavenly nectar, while he served the novice with human food. Once the arhat had finished his meal, he expounded the essential teachings of the Dharma for the nāga king. The novice, as was his custom, washed the bowls for his master. Finding leftover grains in the bowl and being astonished by their fragrance, he immediately gave rise to an evil vow, resenting his master and feeling anger toward the nāga: "May all the power of my merit manifest now, that I may cut off this nāga’s life and become the king myself." At the moment the novice made this vow, the nāga king already felt a headache. The arhat spoke words of instruction and exhortation, and the nāga king apologized for his faults and blamed himself; however, the novice remained resentful and did not follow the instruction to forgive. Once they had returned to the monastery (saṃghārāma), the novice made a vow with utmost sincerity. Due to the power of his merit, he died that very night and was reborn as a great nāga king. Fierce and impetuous, he came to enter the pool, killed the former nāga king, occupied the nāga palace, took possession of his retinue, and assumed command over them. Because of his former vow, he stirred up violent storms and rain, uprooting trees and intending to destroy the monastery. At that time, King Kaniṣka, feeling puzzled, inquired about the matter, and the arhat explained everything to the king. The king then established a monastery (saṃghārāma) for the nāga at the foot of the Snow Mountains and erected a stupa (stūpa) over one hundred feet high. The nāga, harboring his former resentment, proceeded to stir up wind and rain. The king was intent on universal salvation, while the nāga, fueled by the poison of his anger, committed acts of violence, causing the monastery and the stupa to be destroyed six times and rebuilt seven times. King Kaniṣka, ashamed that his work was not being completed, wished to fill in the nāga’s pool and destroy his dwelling; he immediately mobilized his troops and arrived at the foot of the Snow Mountains. At that time, the nāga king, feeling deep fear, transformed himself into an old brahmin, stopped the king’s elephant, and remonstrated, saying: "Great King, you have cultivated good roots in the past and planted many superior causes, which has enabled you to become a human king to whom all submit. Why, then, do you contend with a nāga today? A nāga is merely an animal, a base and vile species, yet he possesses great power and cannot be contested by force. Riding the clouds and driving the wind, treading on the void and walking on water—these are things not controlled by human power; how could they be objects of the king’s wrath? If the king now mobilizes the entire nation to fight against a single nāga, then if you win, the king will gain no prestige for subduing a distant foe, and if you lose, the king will suffer the shame of being defeated by an unworthy opponent. For the sake of the king’s own interests, it would be best to withdraw the troops." King Kaniṣka did not follow this advice. The nāga then returned to the pool, and with a sound like rolling thunder, violent winds uprooted trees, sand and stones fell like rain, clouds and fog obscured the light, and the army’s horses were terrified. The king then took refuge in the Triple Gem and prayed for protection, saying, "By virtue of the many blessings I cultivated in past lives, I became a king of men, deterring powerful enemies and ruling over Jambudvīpa; that I am now humiliated by this dragon beast is truly due to my meager merit. May all the power of my merit manifest at this moment." Immediately, great smoke and flames arose from his two shoulders; the dragon retreated, the wind grew still, and the clouds and fog rolled away. The king ordered his army to each carry one stone to fill the dragon pool. The dragon king transformed back into a Brahmin and entreated the king again, saying, "I am the dragon king of that pool; fearing your majesty, I submit to you. May the king have compassion and forgive my past offenses. The king nurtures and protects all living beings; why would you inflict harm upon me alone? If you kill me, both you and I will fall into the evil realms; you will be guilty of taking a life, and I will harbor a heart of resentment and enmity—karmic retribution is clear, and good and evil are manifest." The king then made a clear covenant with the dragon, stating that if there were any further offenses, he would certainly not forgive them. The dragon said, "Because of my evil karma, I have received a body as a dragon. The nature of a dragon is fierce and evil, and I cannot control myself; if a heart of anger arises, I may forget what has been stipulated. Now that the king is establishing a monastery (saṃghārāma), I dare not destroy it. I will send one person to keep watch on the mountain ridge; if black clouds arise, they must strike the ghaṇṭā (gong) urgently. When I hear that sound, my evil heart will cease." The king thereupon renovated the monastery and built a stūpa, and the practice of watching for clouds continues to this day without interruption. According to the records of predecessors, there is more than one *sheng* of the Tathāgata’s bone and flesh relics inside the stūpa, and the miraculous events associated with them are difficult to describe in detail. Once, smoke suddenly rose from within the stūpa, followed shortly by fierce flames. The people of the time thought the stūpa had been reduced to ashes, but after gazing at it for a long while, the fire died down and the smoke vanished. Then, the relics were seen like a banner of white pearls, circling the central pillar and winding upwards to the edge of the clouds before whirling back down.
li_quote: halted the king’s elephant, and offered a remonstrance to him

issues: 氣序漸溫 rendered "The climate is gradually becoming warmer" (a change over time): 漸 marks that going south one comes into a warmer climate
en_revised: The country of Lampāka (濫波國) is over a thousand *li* in circuit. To the north, it has the Snow Mountains at its back, and on the other three sides, it borders the Black Range (黑嶺). The capital city of the country is over ten *li* in circuit. For several hundred years, the royal lineage has been extinct, and powerful men have contended for strength, leaving the country without a great sovereign; only recently has it become a dependency of the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國). The land is suitable for non-glutinous rice and produces much sugarcane; although trees are numerous, they yield little fruit. The climate begins to be warm, with light frost but no snow. The customs of the country are prosperous and joyful, and the people are fond of singing and chanting; however, their dispositions are timid and weak, their hearts are deceitful, and they engage in mutual deception and mockery, lacking any sense of deference. Their physical stature is small, and their movements are restless. They mostly wear white cotton cloth and their attire is bright and decorative. There are more than ten monasteries with few monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Mahayana. There are several dozen *deva* temples, and the followers of heterodox paths are very numerous.
li_quote: The climate is temperate; there is little frost and no snow.

issues: 無大君長，主令役屬迦畢試國 rendered "There is no great monarch; the ruler is subject to": there is no ruler; 主令 means its government (the sovereign's commands) comes from Kāpiśī, i.e. it is a dependency
en_revised: From here, traveling southeast for over a hundred li, crossing a great mountain range, and fording a large river, one arrives at the country of Nagarahāra (那揭羅曷國) (within the borders of North India). The country of Nagarahāra is over six hundred li from east to west and two hundred and fifty or sixty li from south to north. Mountains surround its four borders, which are precipitous and dangerous. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit. There is no great monarch; it is governed as a dependency of the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國). The land is rich in grain and crops, and there are many flowers and fruits. The climate is warm and hot. The customs of the people are simple and honest; they are fierce, brave, and valiant, valuing wealth lightly and loving learning. They revere and respect the Buddha-Dharma and have little faith in heterodox paths. Although there are many saṃghārāmas, the number of monks is small, and the various stūpas are desolate and ruined. There are five Deva temples and over a hundred followers of heterodox paths.
li_quote: There is no sovereign king to rule over the country and it belongs to Kāpiśī as a vassal state.

issues: 斯五聖迹 rendered "These five sacred sites": the 聖迹 here are the five relics just listed (crown bone, skull, eye, robe, staff) kept in the pavilion, not sites
en_revised: Thirty-some *li* southeast of the city, one arrives at the city of Haḍḍa (醯羅城). It is four or five *li* in circumference, with steep and rugged defenses, and flower groves and ponds that are bright, fresh, and clear as mirrors. The people living in the city are honest, simple, and possess upright faith. There is a multi-storied pavilion with painted beams and vermilion pillars. In the second story of the pavilion is a small stupa made of the seven precious substances, in which the crown bone of the Tathāgata is placed. The bone is one foot and two inches in circumference, with distinct hair pores, and its color is yellowish-white; it is contained in a precious casket and placed inside the stupa. Those who wish to know the signs of their good or evil karma mix incense powder with clay and press it onto the crown bone; according to the response of their merit, the patterns appear clearly. There is another small stupa made of the seven precious substances to store the Tathāgata’s skull bone, which is shaped like a lotus leaf and is the same color as the crown bone; it is also kept sealed within a precious casket. There is another small stupa made of the seven precious substances containing the Tathāgata’s eyeball, which is as large as a *nai* (㮈, crab-apple) fruit, brilliant and transparent, shining through from inside to out; it is also kept sealed within a precious casket. The Tathāgata’s *saṃghāṭī* (monastic robe) is made of fine cotton cloth (㲲), its color is yellowish-red, and it is kept in a precious casket; as the years have been long, it is slightly damaged. The Tathāgata’s *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) has rings made of white iron and a shaft made of sandalwood; it is kept in a precious tube. Recently, a king heard that all these objects were things the Tathāgata had personally used in the past, and relying on his power, he forcibly took them away. Once they arrived in his own country, he placed them in the palace where he resided, but before even twelve days had passed, when he sought them, they were already lost; upon further searching, they had already returned to their original place. These five sacred relics possess many spiritual wonders, and the king of Kapiśa (迦畢試國) has appointed five pure-practitioners (brahmacārins) to provide incense and flowers in service to them. Pilgrims coming to pay their respects arrive in an unbroken succession. The pure-practitioners, desiring to pursue emptiness and tranquility, and considering that wealth is something people value, have provisionally established a schedule of fees to put an end to the clamor and confusion. The general outline is as follows: those who wish to see the Tathāgata’s crown bone must pay a tax of one gold coin; if they wish to take an impression, they must pay a tax of five gold coins; for the remaining items, there is a graded schedule of fees. Although the fees are heavy, the number of those coming to pay their respects only increases. To the northwest of the multi-storied pavilion is a stūpa, which is also very tall and displays many spiritual wonders; if a person touches it with a finger, it immediately begins to shake, its very foundations tilt and move, and its bells ring in harmony.
li_quote: These ﬁve holy objects have shown many spiritual signs.

issues: 初至此國，適遭大火 rendered "I happened to encounter a great fire": it is the stūpa that had just suffered the fire (適遭 continues 成壞已三), and Xuanzang saw it under reconstruction
en_revised: To the south of the Pippala tree is a stupa built by King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王). Four hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, King Kaniṣka ascended the throne and ruled over Jambudvīpa. He did not believe in merit or demerit and slighted the Buddha’s Dharma. While hunting in the marshes, he encountered a white rabbit; the king personally gave chase, but it suddenly vanished at this spot. He saw a young cowherd among the trees making a small stupa three feet in height. The king asked, "What are you doing?" The cowherd replied, "Long ago, the holy wisdom of Śākya Buddha prophesied: 'A king will appear who shall build a stupa on this excellent site, and many of my bodily relics will be gathered within it.' Your Majesty’s holy virtues were cultivated in the past, your name matches the ancient prophecy, and your divine merit and superior fortune are destined for this very moment; therefore, I have come ahead to alert and inspire you." Having said this, he suddenly disappeared. Hearing these words, the king was filled with joy and reverence. Reflecting on his name and the Great Sage’s prior prophecy, he developed true faith and deeply respected the Buddha’s Dharma. Around the small stupa, he built a stone stupa, wishing to use his power to cover it completely. Yet, as he increased the height, the small stupa always emerged three feet above it. Only when the height exceeded four hundred feet—with the base standing one and a half li in circumference and a five-tiered foundation one hundred and fifty feet high—was he finally able to cover the small stupa. The king, rejoicing at this auspicious event, further erected twenty-five tiers of gilded copper rings above it, and placing one hu of the Tathāgata’s relics within them, he performed offerings in this manner. No sooner was the construction finished than he saw the small stupa protruding halfway out from beneath the southeast corner of the great foundation. The king was displeased and cast it away; it then lodged halfway within the stone base under the second tier of the stupa, while another small stupa emerged once more at its original location. The king then withdrew and sighed, saying: "Alas, human efforts are easily misguided, but divine merit is difficult to conceal. When supported by the holy and spiritual, what can anger achieve?" Having felt shame and fear, he confessed his fault and returned. Those two stupas are still present today; those who are afflicted with illness and wish to pray for recovery apply incense and scatter flowers, and with sincere devotion take refuge, most of them obtaining a cure. To the south of the stone steps on the eastern face of the great stupa, two stupas are carved, one three feet high and the other five feet high, their design and shape modeled after the great stupa. Two Buddha images are also fashioned, one four feet high and the other six feet high, imitating the seated image with crossed legs under the Mahā-bodhi tree; when the sunlight shines upon them, the golden color glitters brilliantly, and as the shadows gradually shift, the stone patterns appear dark blue. I have heard from the elders that several hundred years ago, there were golden ants in the crevices of the stone base, the large ones like fingers and the small ones like grains of wheat, which followed one another to gnaw at the stone wall, the patterns appearing as if carved and inlaid with gold sand, forming these images, which are still present today. On the southern side of the stone steps of the great stūpa (大窣堵波) there is a painted Buddha image sixteen feet high; from the chest upward it appears as two bodies, but from the chest downward it is joined into one. I have heard from the records of the ancients that in the beginning, there was a poor man who supported himself by manual labor and, having obtained one gold coin, wished to have a Buddha image made. He went to the place of the stūpa and said to a painter, "I now wish to depict the exquisite features of the Tathāgata (如來), but I have only one gold coin, which is insufficient to reward your labor; I have long cherished this desire but am burdened by worry, being constrained by my poverty." At that time, the painter, perceiving his utmost sincerity, did not speak of the price but promised to complete the work. Later, there was another man whose circumstances were the same as the former; he brought a gold coin and requested that an image of the Buddha be painted. The painter then accepted the money from both men, sought out excellent pigments, and painted a single image for them both. When the two men came on the same day to pay their respects, the painter pointed to the one image, showed it to them, and said, "This is the Buddha image you commissioned." The two men looked at each other, as if they had some misgivings. The painter, knowing their doubts in his heart, said to the two men, "Why are you so long in thought? Whatever I have received, I have not diminished by even a hair's breadth. If these words are not false, the image will surely manifest a divine transformation." Before his voice had ceased, the image manifested a miracle: the bodies separated and their shadows intertwined, and the light of the image shone brilliantly. The two men were convinced and filled with faith and joy. More than a hundred paces to the southwest of the great stupa (mahāstūpa), there is a white stone Buddha image eighteen feet high, standing and facing north; it possesses many divine signs and frequently emits light. At times, people have seen the image go out at night to walk, circumambulating the great stupa. Recently, a group of thieves intended to enter and commit theft, but the image went out to meet them; the band of thieves was terrified and retreated, and the image returned to its original place, standing as before. Because of this, the group of thieves reformed and renewed themselves, traveling through the towns and villages to tell everyone, far and near. To the left and right of the great stupa, there are hundreds of small stupas arranged like fish scales. The Buddha images are adorned with the utmost craftsmanship, and extraordinary fragrances and strange sounds are sometimes heard; divine immortals and sages are occasionally seen circumambulating them. Regarding this stupa, the Tathāgata prophesied that it would be burned seven times and rebuilt seven times, at which point the Buddhadharma would come to an end. The records of the ancients state that it has already been built and destroyed three times. When I first arrived in this country, it had just suffered a great fire, and I saw it being rebuilt, though the work was not yet completed.
li_quote: When I ﬁrst came to this country the stupa had just suffered the disaster of conﬂagration. It is now under repair and the structure is not yet completed.

issues: 谷水西派，逆流東上 rendered as the stream "flows back up eastward against its course": the stream flows west, and it is the traveller who goes up eastward against its current. Also 方石如塔 "resemble pagodas": CBETA's 塔 is a corruption of 榻 "couch" (Ji 1985 from all other witnesses and Huilin's yinyi), matching 宛若工成
en_revised: More than four hundred *li* to the south of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), one reaches Mount Hiḍḍa (醯羅山). The valley stream flows to the west; going up eastward against its current, various flowers and strange fruits cover the gullies and line the cliffs. The peaks and crags are perilous, and the streams and valleys wind and meander; sometimes one hears the sound of loud talking, and sometimes one hears the strains of music. Square stones resemble couches (reading 榻 for CBETA's 塔 "pagoda"), appearing as if fashioned by craftsmen, stretching out in succession and spreading through the cliffs and valleys. This is where the Tathāgata in a former life sacrificed his body and life to hear half a stanza (Formerly it was called *jie* (伽), which is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit. Some call it *jieta* (偈他), which is a corruption of the Sanskrit sound. Following the correct pronunciation now, it should be called *gāthā* (伽他). *Gāthā* means *song* (頌) in the language of Tang, a *song* being thirty-two syllables) of the Dharma.
li_quote: where the stream in the valley ﬂows westward. As one goes up to the east against the current of the stream … Lying linked together in the valley are square rocks that resemble bedsteads made by craftsmen.

issues: 命有讌私，未聞來旨 rendered "Though fate has brought us to intimacy": 命 is the Śākya's request ("you bid me to intimacy, but I have not heard my parents' will"), not fate; also 遂欵殷勤，凌逼野合 rendered "forcing himself upon her", as if accomplished: he presses her to lie with him, and she refuses for want of her parents' consent
en_revised: One hundred and fifty li northwest of the statue of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one arrives at the mountain of Lamboura (藍勃盧山). On the mountain ridge is a dragon lake, over thirty li in circumference; its green waves are vast and expansive, and its clear waters are as bright as a mirror. In the past, when King Virūḍhaka (毘盧釋迦王) attacked the Śākyas, four men resisted the army; they were expelled by their kinsmen and each fled in a different direction. One of these Śākyas, having left the capital, was exhausted from his travels and stopped midway. At that time, a wild goose flew before him; since it was tame and friendly, he mounted it. The goose flew and landed beside this lake. The Śākya, having traveled through the air far to a foreign land, was lost and did not know the way, so he took a nap in the shade of a tree. The young daughter of the dragon of the lake was wandering along the water's edge when she suddenly saw the Śākya; fearing her appearance was inappropriate, she transformed into human form and approached to stroke him. The Śākya was startled awake and asked, "I am a weary traveler, why do you show me such intimacy?" He then pressed her with great earnestness, urging her to lie with him in the wilderness. The woman said, "I have my parents' instructions, which I respect and do not violate. Although I am honored by your attention, I have not received their command." The Śākya asked, "The mountain valleys are dark and remote; where is your home?" She replied, "I am the dragon daughter of this lake. I respectfully heard that your noble clan was wandering in exile, and as I happened to be out for a stroll, I dared to offer comfort for your fatigue. Though you bid me to intimacy, I have not yet heard my parents’ will. Furthermore, due to accumulated karma, I have received this dragon body; humans and animals follow different paths, and such a thing is unheard of." The Śākya said, "If you grant me this one word, my long-held desire will be fulfilled." The dragon girl said, "I respectfully hear your command; I submit to whatever you decide." The Śākya then made a vow in his heart: "By whatever power of merit I possess, let this dragon girl's entire body be transformed into that of a human." Moved by the power of his merit, the dragon then changed her form; having attained a human body, she was deeply overjoyed. She thanked the Śākya, saying, "Due to my accumulated evil karma, I have been wandering in the lower realms. Fortunately, I have received your kind attention, and through the application of your merit, this wretched body held for vast kalpas has been transformed in an instant. I wish to repay this virtue, but even shattering my body would not be enough. I desire to accompany you, but I am constrained by the opinions of others. I wish to inform my parents, and then prepare the rites." The dragon girl returned to the pool and told her parents, "Today while out on an excursion, I suddenly met a member of the Śākya clan; moved by the power of his merit, I have been transformed into a human. My heart is set on a happy union, and I venture to state the facts." The Dragon King, pleased with the human realm and holding the holy clan in high regard, acceded to his daughter's request. He then emerged from the pool and thanked the Śākya, saying, "You have not shunned those of a different species, but have lowered your noble status to accommodate the lowly. I wish for you to visit my dwelling, where I dare to offer you my service." The Śākya accepted the Dragon King's invitation and went to his residence. There, within the dragon palace, they prepared the rites for a personal wedding, and in the joy of their new union, they indulged in the utmost pleasure. However, the Śākya, seeing the dragon's form, felt constant fear and disgust, and wished to take his leave. The Dragon King stopped him, saying, "I hope you will not go far away, but reside in this neighborhood. I shall cause you to occupy territory, bear a great title, command subjects, and enjoy a long-lasting dynasty." The Śākya declined, saying, "This is not what I desire." The Dragon King placed a precious sword into a chest and covered it with a fine white cotton cloth. He said to the Śākya, "I hope you will take this cloth and present it to the king. The king will surely receive this tribute from a man from afar in person, and at that moment, you can slay him. By then seizing his kingdom, would that not be excellent?" The Śākya accepted the dragon’s instructions and went to present it. As the King of Udyāna (烏仗那) personally lifted the cloth, the Śākya seized his sleeve and stabbed him. The attendants and guards were in an uproar on the palace steps, but the Śākya brandished his sword and declared, "The sword I wield was bestowed upon me by the divine dragon to execute those who are slow to submit and to behead those who are not loyal." All were awed by his divine martial prowess and elevated him to the high throne. Thereupon, he reformed the corrupt administration, honored the virtuous, and relieved the suffering. Having done this, he mobilized a great assembly and prepared a royal procession to go to the dragon palace to report his success and bring the dragon girl back to the capital. Because the dragon girl’s past karma was not yet exhausted and residual retribution remained, whenever they were in private, nine dragon heads would emerge from her head. The Śākya, fearful and disgusted, did not know what plan to devise, but when he caught her sleeping, he cut them off with a sharp blade. The dragon girl, startled from her sleep, said, "This is not to the benefit of our descendants; not only is my life somewhat injured, but your offspring shall suffer from headaches." Therefore, the royal clan of this country often suffers from this affliction; although it is not continuous, it flares up from time to time. After the Śākya passed away, his son succeeded to the throne; this was King Uttarasena (嗢呾羅犀那; Tang dynasty translation: "Superior Army"). After King Uttarasena succeeded to the throne, his mother lost her sight. The Tathāgata, having subdued the dragon Apalāla (阿波邏羅), was returning and descended through the air into the palace. King Uttarasena happened to be out hunting, so the Tathāgata briefly explained the essentials of the Dharma to his mother. Having encountered the Holy One and heard the Dharma, she immediately regained her sight. The Tathāgata asked, "Your son is of my clan; where is he now?" The mother replied, "He went out hunting this morning and is now on his way back." The Tathāgata and the great assembly were about to depart. The King’s mother said, "It is only by my good fortune that I gave birth into this holy clan; the Tathāgata has shown great compassion by personally visiting us. My son is just now returning, so I pray you stay and wait a moment." The World-Honored One said, "This man is of my clan. He can be awakened to faith by hearing the teachings; he does not require personal instruction to arouse his resolve. I shall depart. When he returns, tell him: 'The Tathāgata is going from here to the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城) to enter nirvāṇa among the śāla trees; you should obtain the relics and make offerings to them yourself.'" The Tathāgata and the great assembly then rose into the void and departed. King Uttarasena was out hunting and saw from afar a brilliant light shining in the palace; suspecting a fire, he stopped his hunt and returned. He then saw that his mother had regained her sight, and he asked joyfully, "How long was I gone that such an auspicious response occurred, restoring my mother's vision as it was before?" The mother replied, "After you went out, the Tathāgata arrived here; upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, I regained my sight." "The Tathāgata has gone from here to the śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城) to enter nirvana; he summons you to come quickly to receive a portion of his relics." When the king heard this, he wailed with grief and collapsed to the ground. After a long time, he regained his senses and ordered his carriage to hasten to the site. By the time he arrived between the twin trees, the Buddha had already entered nirvana. At that time, the various kings looked down upon his borderland status and, treasuring the relics, did not wish to share them with him. Then, the assembly of devas and humans restated the Buddha’s intention; having heard this, the kings divided the relics equally, giving him his share first.
li_quote: You ask me to have intimacy with you but I have not received instructions from my parents.

issues: 其訖利多種屢以僧徒覆宗滅祀 rendered "the Kṛta tribe had frequently caused the ruin of clans and the extinction of sacrifices on account of the monks": the Kṛtas are the sufferers, their own line overthrown and ancestral sacrifices cut off (by Aśoka, Kaniṣka, Himatala) because of the monks; hence their grudge
en_revised: From here, traveling southeast, climbing mountains and traversing dangerous paths, crossing an iron bridge, and journeying more than one thousand li, one arrives at the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) (formerly called Jibin [罽賓], which is a corruption; it is in the territory of Northern India). The country of Kaśmīra is over seven thousand li in circumference. Its four borders are backed by mountains; the mountains are extremely steep and precipitous. Although there are gateways and paths, they are narrow and constricted, and since ancient times, neighboring enemies have been unable to attack or conquer it. The capital city of the country faces a great river to the west, measuring twelve or thirteen li from north to south and four or five li from east to west. It is suitable for agriculture, abounds in flowers and fruits, and produces dragon-breed horses, saffron (鬱金香), fire pearls, and medicinal herbs. The climate is cold and harsh, with much snow and little wind. The people wear woolen garments and white cotton (白㲲) clothing. The local customs are frivolous, and the people are mostly timid and cowardly. The country is protected by a dragon, and thus it has become powerful among its neighbors. The people are beautiful in appearance but deceitful in nature. They are fond of learning and are well-informed, believing in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas and more than five thousand monks. There are four stūpas, all built by King Aśoka (無憂王), each containing over a pint of the Tathāgata’s relics. The *Country Records* (國志) state: "The land of this country was originally a dragon lake. In the past, when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had subdued an evil spirit in the country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國) and wished to return to the Middle Kingdom, he rode through the air and, upon reaching the space above this country, said to Ānanda: 'After my parinirvāṇa, there will be an arhat named Madhyāntika (末田底迦) who will establish a kingdom in this land, settle the people, and propagate the Buddha-dharma.'" In the fiftieth year after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the arhat Madhyāntika (末田底迦), a disciple of Ānanda, having attained the six supernatural powers and possessing the eight liberations, heard the Buddha’s prediction and felt great joy in his heart. He then came to this place, sat in meditation within the woods of the great mountain range (大山), and manifested great supernatural transformations. The dragon saw this and, having developed deep faith, asked what he desired. The arhat said, "I wish for you to grant me enough space within this lake to accommodate my knees." The dragon king thereupon caused the water to recede and offered the land to him. The arhat used his supernatural power to expand his body, and the dragon king exerted his strength to shrink the water; when the lake was empty and the water exhausted, the dragon turned and asked for the land back. The arhat left one pool for him in the northwest of this place, measuring one hundred and more li in circumference; the rest of his kin and dependents were to dwell in smaller pools separately. The dragon king said, "I have bestowed the entire lake and land upon you; I wish to provide offerings perpetually." Madhyāntika replied, "I shall soon enter parinirvāṇa without remainder; though I wish to accept your invitation, how would that be possible?" The dragon king requested again, "May five hundred arhats always receive my offerings until the Dharma comes to an end; after the Dharma has ended, I shall take back this country to serve as my dwelling pool." Madhyāntika acceded to his request. Once the arhat had obtained the land, he employed his great supernatural power to establish five hundred monasteries (伽藍). He purchased people of low status from various other countries to serve as laborers and provide for the monastic community. After Madhyāntika entered parinirvāṇa, those low-status people established their own leader. The neighboring countries despised their lowly caste and would not intermarry with them, calling them Kṛta (translated into Chinese as "bought"). At the present time, the spring water has already overflowed in many places. In the hundredth year after the Tathāgata’s nirvana, King Aśoka (無憂王) of the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) ascended the throne and ruled the world; his majesty extended to distant lands. He had deep faith in the Three Jewels and cherished and nurtured the four types of living beings. At that time, there were five hundred arhat monks and five hundred ordinary monks, all of whom the king revered and supported without distinction. There was an ordinary monk named Mahādeva (摩訶提婆; translated into Chinese as "Great Heaven" [大天]), who was broad-minded and highly intelligent. He sought deeply into name and reality and composed a treatise through profound reflection that contradicted the holy teachings; those who heard of it followed his heterodox views. King Aśoka, unable to distinguish between the ordinary and the holy, sympathized with those he liked and sided with those close to him; he summoned the monks to the Ganges River (殑伽河), intending to drown them in the deep current and execute them all. When the arhats were faced with this mortal danger, they all exercised their supernatural powers, ascended into the void, and walked through the air, coming to this country to dwell in the mountains and hide in the valleys. When King Aśoka heard of this, he was afraid; he came in person to apologize and requested them to return to their own country. The arhats firmly refused to comply. King Aśoka built five hundred monasteries (伽藍) for the arhats and bestowed this entire country upon the community of monks. In the four-hundredth year after the Tathāgata’s nirvana, King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) of the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) ascended the throne in accordance with the prophesied time; his royal influence spread far and wide, and people of diverse customs came to submit to his rule. In his leisure time from state affairs, he would study the Buddhist scriptures, daily inviting a monk to the palace to expound the Dharma. However, the various schools held divergent views, and the king was deeply perplexed, finding no way to resolve his doubts. At that time, the Venerable Pārśva (脇尊者) said: "Since the Tathāgata passed away, the years have grown distant; the disciples have formed different schools, and teachers have held divergent views, each relying on what they have heard and seen, and all contradicting one another." When the king heard this, he was deeply moved and grieved; after sighing in lamentation for a long while, he said to the Venerable: "By my humble remaining merit, I have followed in the footsteps of my predecessors; though far removed from the Sage, I am still fortunate. Venturing to forget my own unworthiness, I wish to promote and exalt the Dharma, explaining the Tripiṭaka in full according to the tenets of the various schools." The Venerable Pārśva said: "Your Majesty has planted roots of goodness in past lives and is richly endowed with blessings; that you should devote your mind to the Buddha-dharma is exactly what I desire." The king then issued a decree to near and far, summoning the sages and philosophers. Thereupon, they gathered from the four directions, traveling like stars across ten thousand miles; the brilliant and the wise all assembled. For seven days, he provided the four requisites as offerings. Wishing to hold a doctrinal discussion, he feared it would be noisy and chaotic. The king then expressed his thoughts to the monks, saying: "Those who have attained the fruits of sainthood may stay; those who are still bound by worldly fetters shall return." Even so, the number remained large. He issued another order: "Those who are 'without learning' (aśaikṣa) may stay; those who are 'still learning' (śaikṣa) shall return." Still, they were numerous. He issued yet another order: "Those who possess the three insights and are equipped with the six supernatural powers may stay; all others shall return." Yet, they were still numerous. He issued another order: "Those who have internally mastered the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka) and externally attained the Five Sciences (pañcavidyā) may stay; all others shall return." Thereupon, four hundred and ninety-nine people were obtained. The king wished to hold the assembly in his own country, but he was troubled by its heat and humidity; he also wished to go to the stone cave in Rājagṛha where Mahākāśyapa had conducted the council. The Venerable Pārśva and the others deliberated, saying: "That is not possible. There are many non-Buddhists there, and their divergent views are tangled and confusing; one would be too busy responding to them to have any energy to compose the treatise. The hearts of the assembly are set on this country. This country is surrounded by solid mountains, guarded by yakṣas, its land is fertile, and its products are abundant; it is a place where sages and saints gather, and where spiritual immortals roam and dwell." The assembly deliberated on this, and all said: "This is appropriate." At that time, the king and the arhats arrived from there, established a monastery, and compiled the Tripiṭaka, intending to compose the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*. At that time, the Venerable Vasumitra was outside the door mending his robes. The arhats said to Vasumitra: "Your fetters (kleśa) are not yet removed, and your pure deliberations are erroneous; you should go far away and not stay here." Vasumitra replied: "You worthies have no doubts regarding the Dharma; you act on behalf of the Buddha to transform others, and are now gathering the great meaning, wishing to compose a correct treatise. Although I am not clever, I have a rough understanding of the subtle words; I have also studied deeply the profound texts of the Tripiṭaka and the ultimate principles of the Five Sciences, and have grasped their essence." The arhats said: "Words cannot be like this. You should withdraw and dwell apart, quickly attain the state of 'no-learning' (aśaikṣa), and then join us; it will not be too late." Vasumitra said, "I regard the state of 'no-learning' (aśaikṣa) as I would spit or mucus; my aspiration is to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, not to pursue the lesser path. I shall throw this ball of thread, and before it falls to the ground, I shall certainly attain the holy fruit of 'no-learning'." At that time, the arhats rebuked him again, saying, "This is what is called a person of excessive pride. The fruit of 'no-learning' is praised by all Buddhas; you should attain it quickly to resolve the doubts of the assembly." Thereupon, Vasumitra threw the ball of thread. The devas in the air caught the ball of thread and pleaded, "You are about to realize the fruit of Buddhahood and will next succeed Maitreya (慈氏); as the most honored one in the three realms and the one upon whom all beings of the four births depend, why do you wish to realize the lesser fruit here?" When the arhats saw this event, they apologized for their fault, acknowledged his virtue, and invited him to be the chairperson; whenever there were doubts or discussions, they all took his decision as final. These five hundred sages first composed the *Upadeśa-śāstra* (鄔波第鑠論) (The old name, *Upadeśa-śāstra* (優波提舍論), is a corruption) in one hundred thousand stanzas, explaining the *Sūtra-piṭaka* (素呾纜藏) (The old name, *Sūtra-piṭaka* (修多羅藏), is a corruption). Next, they composed the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (毘柰耶毘婆沙論) in one hundred thousand stanzas, explaining the *Vinaya-piṭaka* (毘奈耶藏) (The old name, *Vinaya-piṭaka* (毘那耶藏), is a corruption). Finally, they composed the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (阿毘達磨毘婆沙論) in one hundred thousand stanzas, explaining the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (阿毘達磨藏) (Or it is called *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (阿毘曇藏), which is an abbreviation). In total, there are three hundred thousand stanzas and nine million six hundred thousand words, providing a complete explanation of the Tripiṭaka to be preserved for all eternity; they exhaustively explore every branch and detail, investigating both the shallow and the deep, so that the great principles are clarified once more, the subtle words are again revealed, and through their wide circulation, later students may rely upon them. King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) then had the treatises incised on red copper plates, sealed them in stone cases, and erected a stūpa to store them inside. He commanded Yakṣa deities to guard the country, not allowing those of other schools to take these treatises out; those who wished to study them were to receive instruction within the country. When this work was completed, he returned his army to his capital. He went outside the western gate of this country, knelt facing east, and once again bestowed this entire country upon the community of monks. After King Kaniṣka passed away, the Kṛta (訖利多) tribe again claimed the kingship, expelled the monks, and destroyed the Buddha-dharma. The King of Himatala (呬摩呾羅王) (In the language of the Tang, "under the snow mountains") in the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國) was a descendant of the Śākya clan. Six hundred years after the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa, he came to possess vast territories and inherited the royal enterprise; he planted his heart in the soil of the Buddha and poured his sentiments into the sea of the Dharma. Hearing that the Kṛta had destroyed the Buddha-dharma, he gathered three thousand brave warriors from his country, disguised them as merchants, and, carrying many precious goods while concealing weapons, entered this country. The king of this country treated them with special courtesy. From among the merchants, he further selected five hundred men who were fierce and resourceful; each hid a sharp blade in his sleeve and carried heavy treasures, personally bearing their offerings to present them to the king. At that moment, the King of Himatala (雪山下王) removed his cap and took the throne. The King of the Kṛta (訖利多王) was paralyzed with terror, whereupon the king beheaded him and commanded the subordinates, saying: "I am the King of Himatala in the country of Tukhāra (覩邏國). I am enraged by this base race’s public practice of tyrannical government, and therefore I have executed the guilty one today. As for all you common people, this is not your crime." However, he relocated the country’s ministers and officials to a foreign territory. Having pacified this country, he summoned the monks, established monasteries, and restored peace and order as before. Furthermore, outside the western gate of this country, he knelt facing east and offered alms to the assembly of monks. Because the Kṛta tribe had repeatedly seen their line overthrown and their ancestral sacrifices cut off on account of the monks, they had accumulated resentment for generations and detested the Buddha-dharma. As time passed, they again proclaimed themselves kings. Therefore, this country does not hold the faith in high esteem today, and they pay special attention to the temples of the non-Buddhist gods.
li_quote: Because the Krīta tribesmen had lost power on account of Buddhist monks on several occasions, they bore them a grudge for generations and hated the buddha-dharma.

issues: 眾人聞之，相更譏笑 rendered "they mocked one another": 相更 here is "mocked him all the more" (the jeering is aimed at the arhat, continuing 時人譏曰)
en_revised: More than ten li to the east of the Buddha-tooth monastery, among the cliffs of the northern mountains, there is a small monastery where the great master of shastras Skandhila (索建地羅) once composed the *Prakaraṇapāda-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (眾事分毘婆沙論). In the small monastery there is a stone stūpa over fifty feet high, which contains the bodily relics of an arhat. Previously, there was an arhat whose physical form was immense, and all that he ate was equal to that of an elephant. The people of the time ridiculed him, saying, "You only know how to eat your fill; how could you understand right from wrong?" When the arhat was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he told the people, "I shall soon attain the state of no-remainder; I wish to speak of the wonderful Dharma that I have personally realized." When the people heard this, they mocked him all the more, and they all gathered together to observe his success or failure. Then the arhat said to the people, "I will now tell you the original cause and condition. Prior to this life, I received the retribution of an elephant's body in East India, where I lived in the king's inner stable. At that time, there was a śramaṇa of this country who traveled far to India to search for the scriptures and treatises of the holy teachings. The king took me and gave me to the śramaṇa to carry the Buddhist scriptures, and in this way, I arrived here. Not long after, I died. By virtue of the merit accumulated through carrying the scriptures, I was born as a human. Furthermore, blessed with remaining fortune, I donned the dyed robes early and diligently sought liberation, never resting, until I attained the six supernatural powers and severed the desires of the three realms. However, regarding what I eat, the residual habit remains; I always restrain myself, eating only one-third of what I once did." Although there was this account, people still did not believe it. He then ascended into the void, entered the fire-light samādhi (火光定), and smoke and flames issued from his body as he entered parinirvāṇa; his remaining bones fell to the ground, and a stūpa (窣堵波) was erected over them.
li_quote: On hearing this the people all jeered at him even more and they all gathered to see what would happen.
